claims.text: Conventionally processed high-entropy alloys often have homogeneous or inadequately tailored microstructures associated with mechanical-property trade-offs.
Severe plastic deformation followed by spatially controlled gradient annealing can generate a hierarchical microstructure containing nanoscale grains and a controlled secondary-phase distribution.
The proposed treatment can simultaneously improve yield strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
Preservation of the nanograined structure and prevention of phase instability are necessary for the proposed benefits.
Complete homogenization during annealing would make the treatment ineffective.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure may cause grain coarsening and loss of the proposed benefits.
A hierarchical microstructure combining fine grain boundaries with a duplex or lamellar secondary-phase network can provide reinforcement and strain accommodation.
Grain refinement increases yield strength by impeding dislocation motion.
A controlled heterogeneous or secondary-phase network can retain or enhance ductility through strain partitioning, interfacial strain gradients, and constraint effects.
Back-stress strengthening contributes to the proposed strength-ductility balance.
Strain partitioning and back-stress strengthening can maintain or optimize Young's modulus.
The treatment is expected to improve yield strength by approximately 20–30% relative to conventionally processed HEAs.
The treatment is expected to improve fracture toughness by approximately 20–30% relative to conventionally processed HEAs.
The treatment is expected to retain or slightly enhance ductility.
The treatment is expected to maintain or optimize Young's modulus.
Conventional casting and rolling typically optimize one mechanical property at the expense of others.
Failure to reproducibly form the intended hierarchical microstructure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis requires an improvement in Young's modulus, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule allow Young's modulus merely to be maintained.

The boundary states that the property claim applies only when the intended hierarchical microstructure is generated, but the falsification rule treats failure to generate that microstructure as falsification of the causal hypothesis rather than as failure to implement the intervention successfully.
